book.title: North African Jewry in the Twentieth Century: The Jews of Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria

evidence: academic press signal: New York University Press / New York University Press

argument.statement: North African Jewish history was shaped by Zionist activity, emigration to Israel, and antisemitic measures and violence amid colonial rule and nationalist struggles.

book.summary: A history of the Maghreb Jews, stressing Zionist activities and emigration to the State of Israel. Ch. 2 (pp. 55-83), "Under Vichy and the Nazi-German Menace: The Jews of North Africa during the 1930s and 1940s, " deals with anti-Jewish measures (legislation, restrictions, and internment) taken by the Germans and Vichy French authorities, and also in Spanish-occupied Tangier. Antisemitism in the prewar period was aroused by the French, and also broke out during the 1936-39 riots in Palestine. After the war, it was manifested in bloody incidents in 1948, such as pogroms in Oujda and in Djerada in Morocco. Arab nationalists were hostile to Jews because of the latters' support for Zionism and emigration to Israel, and because of their alleged lack of identification with Arab national goals. Antisemitic incidents occurred in 1952-56, when the struggle for national independence intensified (in Algeria), and in 1967, in the wake of the Arab-Israeli war.
